steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our CLAMP paper, which prompt-tunes an LLM with a contrastive loss so it can replace CLIP's text encoder. Show that multimodal LLMs are bad at zero-shot classification, give our hypothesis for why, describe the method and its main results, and end with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Multimodal LLMs and what they do well
- The surprise: mLLMs are poor zero-shot classifiers
- Hypothesis: training objective, not capability
- Our method CLAMP and what it achieves
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- mLLMs
  - LLMs went from interesting to extremely useful in past several years
  - adapted to images: map frozen visual backbone to continuous token as LLM input
  - LLaVA (cite), MiniGPT (cite), Instruct-BLIP (cite), GPT-4V (cite): strong captioning and QA
  - use LLM world knowledge for common sense Qs, e.g. why a photo is unusual (Fig. 1 left)
- Classification problem
  - expect world knowledge to help classification too, e.g. type of car (Fig. 1); LLM can describe what cars look like
  - question: can mLLMs do zero-shot classification? given vehicle types + image, which one?
  - answer: surprisingly, not well
  - SOTA mLLMs under 10% top-1 on Stanford Cars (cite) vs CLIP over 80% (Tab. 1)
  - even though best mLLM classification computes likelihood per image-label pair -> many LLM passes, inefficient (Section 4.2, Runtime)
  - counter-intuitive: LLMs proven to encode extensive world knowledge; classification is fundamental, want it in foundation model
- Hypothesis
  - not lack of LLM capability but improper training; generative captioning / instruction-tuning objectives don't enable classification
  - intuition: strong language prior can help VQA even without image features; correct answer may just have higher likelihood
  - Visual GPT-Score (cite): SoTA on several vision-language benchmarks ignoring image, only text likelihood
- CLAMP
  - generative training not enough for discriminative tasks, but LLMs encode useful knowledge
  - replace text encoder of vision-language pretrained model like CLIP (cite) with an LLM
  - Contrastive LAnguage Model Prompt-tuning (CLAMP) (Fig. 2)
  - update minority of LLM params -> approaches zero-shot CLIP trained on much larger data; beats text encoder from scratch on same data (LiT, cite)
  - LiT found pre-trained (smaller) LMs not helpful for zero-shot English classification; we find finetuning modern LLMs helps, esp. on datasets poorly covered in contrastive training data
  - mostly retain generative abilities -> universal generative + discriminative models
  - parameter-efficient finetuning, same base LLM as instruction-tuned mLLMs -> swap CLAMP params with LLaVA's; captioning, VQA, chat, classification with one LLM (Fig. 1)
- Contributions
  - SOTA mLLMs neither accurate nor efficient at zero-shot classification
  - adapter modules trained with contrastive loss; LLM replaces text encoder in contrastive VL model
  - LLM init helps under-represented domains; CLAMP retains generative abilities

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Over the past several years Large Language Models (LLMs) have gone from interesting to extremely useful. Recent work has adapted LLMs to multimodal inputs such as images by learning a mapping from a frozen visual backbone to a continuous token that is used as input to the LLM. These multimodal LLMs (mLLMs) include LLaVA, MiniGPT, Instruct-BLIP, and GPT-4V, and they are impressive at image captioning and question answering. For example, they can use the world knowledge of the LLM to answer common sense questions well, like why a photo is unusual (Fig. 1 left).

You might assume that the LLM's world knowledge would help in the same way with classifying objects into categories, such as what type of car is in the image (Fig. 1). An LLM can after all give a detailed description of what different cars look like. So in this paper we ask whether multimodal LLMs can also do zero-shot classification tasks. For example, if we give an mLLM a list of vehicle types and an image, can it identify which type of vehicle is there? Surprisingly, the answer is that it does not do it well. State-of-the-art mLLMs get under 10% top-1 classification accuracy on Stanford Cars, while CLIP gets over 80% (Tab. 1). And this is even though the best classification algorithm for current mLLMs computes the likelihood for every image-label pair, which needs many passes through the LLM and is inefficient (see Section 4.2, Runtime). This poor classification performance is counter-intuitive, since LLMs have been proven to encode a lot of knowledge about the world. Also, visual classification is a fundamental computer vision task, and it is a capability we definitely want a foundation model to have.

- Hypothesis
  - not lack of LLM capability, improper training; generative captioning / instruction-tuning objectives don't give classification
  - language prior can help VQA without image features; correct answer may just be more likely
  - Visual GPT-Score: SoTA on several benchmarks ignoring the image, only text likelihood
- CLAMP
  - replace text encoder of a model like CLIP with an LLM; Contrastive LAnguage Model Prompt-tuning (Fig. 2)
  - update minority of params -> near zero-shot CLIP (much larger data), beats from-scratch text encoder on same data (LiT)
  - LiT: smaller pre-trained LMs didn't help; ours: finetuned modern LLMs help, esp. datasets poorly covered in contrastive data
  - generative abilities mostly retained
  - parameter-efficient, same base LLM as mLLMs -> swap params with LLaVA; captioning, VQA, chat, classification (Fig. 1)
- Contributions
  - mLLMs neither accurate nor efficient at zero-shot classification
  - contrastive adapter modules let LLM replace text encoder
  - LLM init helps under-represented domains; generative abilities retained

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Over the past several years Large Language Models (LLMs) have gone from interesting to extremely useful. Recent work has adapted LLMs to multimodal inputs such as images by learning a mapping from a frozen visual backbone to a continuous token that is used as input to the LLM. These multimodal LLMs (mLLMs) include LLaVA, MiniGPT, Instruct-BLIP, and GPT-4V, and they are impressive at image captioning and question answering. For example, they can use the world knowledge of the LLM to answer common sense questions well, like why a photo is unusual (Fig. 1 left).

You might assume that the LLM's world knowledge would help in the same way with classifying objects into categories, such as what type of car is in the image (Fig. 1). An LLM can after all give a detailed description of what different cars look like. So in this paper we ask whether multimodal LLMs can also do zero-shot classification tasks. For example, if we give an mLLM a list of vehicle types and an image, can it identify which type of vehicle is there? Surprisingly, the answer is that it does not do it well. State-of-the-art mLLMs get under 10% top-1 classification accuracy on Stanford Cars, while CLIP gets over 80% (Tab. 1). And this is even though the best classification algorithm for current mLLMs computes the likelihood for every image-label pair, which needs many passes through the LLM and is inefficient (see Section 4.2, Runtime). This poor classification performance is counter-intuitive, since LLMs have been proven to encode a lot of knowledge about the world. Also, visual classification is a fundamental computer vision task, and it is a capability we definitely want a foundation model to have.

Our hypothesis is that this weakness does not come from a lack of capability in the LLM but from improper training, and that the generative captioning and instruction-tuning objectives do not allow effective classification. For some intuition, LLMs have a powerful language prior that can improve visual-question answering even without image features. For example, the correct answer might just have higher likelihood in the language model, as Visual GPT-Score illustrates. That work showed that SoTA performance on several vision-language benchmarks can be reached by ignoring the context image completely and only computing the likelihood of the text sequences with the language model.

Since we hypothesize that generative training is not enough for discriminative image tasks, but that LLMs still encode knowledge that is useful for them, we propose to replace the text encoder of a vision-language pretrained model like CLIP with an LLM. We call the method Contrastive LAnguage Model Prompt-tuning (CLAMP) (Fig. 2). We find that by updating a minority of the LLM parameters, our method can get close to the performance of zero-shot CLIP, which was trained on much larger scale data, and it outperforms a text-encoder trained from scratch on the same data (LiT). This shows the benefits of using Large Language Models. LiT had found earlier that initializing to pre-trained (but smaller scale) LMs does not help zero-shot classification in English. We find instead that carefully finetuning modern, large language models helps compared to training a text-encoder from scratch, especially on evaluation datasets that are poorly covered in the contrastive training data. Surprisingly, we can also mostly keep the generative capabilities of the language model, which points towards universal generative and discriminative models. Finally, we use parameter-efficient finetuning methods and the same base LLM as current instruction-tuned mLLMs, so our method makes it possible to swap CLAMP's finetuned parameters with those of mLLMs like LLaVA. As shown in Fig. 1, this allows captioning, VQA, chat and classification with the same foundational LLM.

To summarize, our contributions are:

- We show that SOTA multimodal LLMs are not accurate and not efficient at zero-shot image classification.

- We train a set of adapter modules with a contrastive loss. They let an LLM be used for visual discrimination tasks by replacing the text encoder in a contrastive vision-language model.

- We show that the LLM initialization in CLAMP improves performance in domains that are under-represented in the pre-training data, and that CLAMP keeps its generative abilities even after our fine-tuning.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the past several years the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have progressed from interesting to extremely useful. Recent work has adapted LLMs to multimodal inputs such as images by learning a mapping from a frozen visual backbone to a continuous token used as input to the LLM. Such multimodal LLMs (mLLMs) include LLaVA [1], MiniGPT [3], Instruct-BLIP [4], and GPT-4V [5], and they have impressive image captioning and question-answering capabilities. For example, they can use the LLM's world knowledge to effectively answer common sense questions, such as why a photo is unusual (Fig. 1 left).

One might assume that the LLM's world knowledge would similarly help in classifying objects into categories, such as what type of car is in the image (Fig. 1); after all, an LLM can provide a detailed description of what different cars look like. In this paper we ask: can multimodal LLMs also perform zero-shot classification tasks? For instance, given a list of vehicle types and an image, can an mLLM identify which type of vehicle is present? We find that the answer is, surprisingly, not well. State-of-the-art mLLMs get under 10% top-1 classification accuracy on Stanford Cars [6], while CLIP achieves over 80% (Tab. 1). This is despite the fact that the best classification algorithm for current mLLMs computes the likelihood for each image-label pair, inefficiently requiring many passes through the LLM (see Section 4.2, Runtime). The poor classification performance of mLLMs is counter-intuitive, since LLMs have been proven to encode extensive knowledge about the world. Moreover, visual classification is a fundamental computer vision task and a capability we definitely want a foundation model to have.

We hypothesize that this weakness is due not to a lack of capability of the LLM but to improper training, and that the generative captioning and instruction-tuning objectives do not enable effective classification. To build intuition for this, consider that LLMs contain a powerful language prior which may improve visual-question answering even without image features; the correct answer may simply have higher likelihood in the language model, as illustrated by Visual GPT-Score [7]. That work showed that SoTA performance can be achieved on several vision-language benchmarks by ignoring the context image completely and computing the likelihood of the text sequences using the language model alone.

Given our hypothesis that generative training is not sufficient for discriminative image tasks, but that LLMs still encode knowledge useful for those tasks, we propose to replace the text encoder of a vision-language pretrained model like CLIP [2] with an LLM. We call our method Contrastive LAnguage Model Prompt-tuning (CLAMP) (Fig. 2). We find that by updating a minority of the LLM parameters, our method can approach the performance of zero-shot CLIP trained on much larger scale data, while outperforming a text-encoder trained from scratch on the same data (LiT [8]). This highlights the benefits of using Large Language Models: LiT earlier found that initializing to pre-trained (but smaller scale) LMs is not helpful for zero-shot classification in English, whereas we find that carefully finetuning modern, large language models helps relative to training a text-encoder from scratch, especially on evaluation datasets with poor coverage in the contrastive training data. Surprisingly, we are also able to mostly retain the generative capabilities of the language model, pointing towards universal generative and discriminative models. Finally, because we use parameter-efficient finetuning methods and the same base LLM as current instruction-tuned mLLMs, our method makes it possible to swap CLAMP's finetuned parameters with those of mLLMs like LLaVA. As illustrated in Fig. 1, this enables captioning, VQA, chat and classification with the same foundational LLM.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

- We show that SOTA multimodal LLMs are neither accurate nor efficient at zero-shot image classification.

- We train a set of adapter modules with a contrastive loss, which enable an LLM to be used for visual discrimination tasks by replacing the text encoder in a contrastive vision-language model.

- We show that the LLM initialization in CLAMP improves performance in domains under-represented in the pre-training data, and that CLAMP retains its generative abilities despite our fine-tuning.
